claims.text: Controlled isothermal aging just below the alloy's ordering transition will induce nanoscale precipitate formation or phase separation.
Nanoscale precipitates act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Increasing domain-wall pinning raises the coercive field relative to an untreated homogeneous baseline.
The aging treatment will produce a measurable increase in coercive field.
The eligible baseline is an as-cast or solution-treated magnetic high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous microstructure.
The comparison should use an untreated sample from the same initial alloy state.
Coercivity should be measured at room temperature using identical field sweep rates for treated and baseline samples.
The effect is expected only in magnetic high-entropy alloys that have an ordering transition and can form nanoscale precipitates.
Precise aging temperature and time control is critical for inducing the desired phase separation without destabilizing the alloy's overall phase balance.
Processing can promote formation of a secondary precipitate phase in a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
Dissolution of precipitates that pin domain walls produces magnetic softening in CoCrFeNiGa0.5.
Similar microstructural tailoring through compositional modification has enhanced coercivity.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase from an isolated thermal aging treatment remains unquantified.
TEM or high-resolution SEM can test whether the treated samples contain the anticipated nanoscale precipitates.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to matched controls would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the anticipated nanoscale precipitates would falsify the proposed aging-to-precipitation pathway.
